topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under RPL Section 442-b, when a salesperson's association with a broker ends, who is responsible for promptly reporting that discontinuance to DOS?
choice_b: The salesperson alone, with no broker reporting duty at all
choice_c: DOS discovers discontinuances automatically with no reporting by anyone
choice_d: The county clerk where the brokerage's office is located
explanation: RPL Section 442-b places the reporting duty on the broker: when a salesperson's association ends, the broker must promptly inform DOS following prescribed procedures -- and if the salesperson moves to a new broker, that new broker must separately report the change.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-b (Discontinuance or change of salesperson's association; report)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under RPL Section 442-b, until a salesperson whose association has ended becomes associated with a new licensed broker, what is that salesperson barred from doing?
choice_a: Performing any act within the prohibitions of Article 12-A -- effectively, engaging in real estate brokerage activity at all
choice_b: Nothing -- the salesperson may continue working exactly as before with no restriction
choice_c: Only renewing their own license, with no restriction on active brokerage work
choice_d: Only showing rental properties, while sales activity remains permitted
explanation: RPL Section 442-b provides that a salesperson may not perform any act within the prohibitions of Article 12-A from the moment their association terminates until they become associated with a new licensed broker -- underscoring that a salesperson has no independent authority to practice real estate brokerage while unaffiliated.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-b (Discontinuance of association -- activity bar while unaffiliated)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under RPL Section 442-b, what fee accompanies a new broker's report to DOS that a salesperson has changed association to that broker?
choice_c: No fee is charged for reporting a change of association
explanation: RPL Section 442-b sets a modest one-dollar fee accompanying the new broker's required report of a salesperson's change of association -- a low administrative charge relative to the $185/$65 initial licensing fees discussed elsewhere.

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under RPL Section 442-c, when may a broker's license be revoked or suspended based solely on a violation committed by that broker's salesperson?
choice_a: Only if the broker had actual knowledge of the violation, or retains the benefits, profits, or proceeds of a transaction wrongfully negotiated by the salesperson after being notified of the misconduct
choice_b: Automatically, any time any salesperson associated with the broker commits any violation, regardless of the broker's knowledge
choice_c: Never -- a broker can never face discipline for a salesperson's individual violation under any circumstance
choice_d: Only if the violation occurred more than five years after the salesperson's initial licensure
explanation: RPL Section 442-c protects a broker from automatic vicarious discipline for a salesperson's violation -- the broker's own license is at risk only where the broker had actual knowledge of the violation, or retained the benefits/profits/proceeds of a wrongfully negotiated transaction after being notified of the misconduct.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-c (Violations by salespersons; broker's responsibility)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under RPL Section 442-c, what criminal classification applies to a broker who knowingly employs a salesperson lacking the required license for that position?
choice_b: A civil infraction only, with no criminal exposure
choice_c: A felony carrying a mandatory prison term
choice_d: No penalty is specified -- the practice is technically unregulated
explanation: RPL Section 442-c makes it a misdemeanor for a broker to employ any salesperson who lacks the license required for that role, independent of the separate 'actual knowledge / retained benefit' standard that governs a broker's discipline exposure for a properly licensed salesperson's individual misconduct.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-c (misdemeanor for employing an unlicensed salesperson)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A broker learns that a salesperson wrongfully negotiated a transaction in violation of Article 12-A, but the broker takes no corrective action and keeps the brokerage's share of the resulting commission. Under RPL Section 442-c, what is the significance of the broker retaining that commission after notification?
choice_a: It can itself support discipline against the broker, since Section 442-c ties broker exposure to retaining the benefits/profits/proceeds of a wrongfully negotiated transaction after notice of the misconduct
choice_b: It is legally irrelevant, since only the salesperson who committed the violation can ever be disciplined
choice_c: It automatically converts the violation into a civil-only matter with no misdemeanor exposure for anyone
choice_d: It has significance only if the commission exceeds $50,000
explanation: Section 442-c specifically identifies retaining the benefits, profits, or proceeds of a wrongfully negotiated transaction -- after being notified of the underlying misconduct -- as one of the two paths (along with actual knowledge) by which a broker's own license can become exposed to discipline for a salesperson's violation.

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: How do RPL Section 442-c's 'actual knowledge or retained benefit' standard and 19 NYCRR Section 175.21's affirmative supervisory duty work together to shape a broker's overall exposure for a salesperson's misconduct?
choice_a: Section 442-c limits when a broker can be disciplined purely for a salesperson's individual violation, while Section 175.21 separately and independently exposes the broker to discipline for failing to provide the required regular, frequent supervision in the first place -- a broker can face 175.21 exposure even without meeting 442-c's knowledge/benefit standard
choice_b: The two provisions are identical and redundant, addressing exactly the same conduct in exactly the same way
choice_c: Section 442-c completely overrides and nullifies the Section 175.21 supervisory duty
choice_d: Neither provision has any bearing on broker discipline; only DOS's informal internal policy governs the outcome
explanation: These are two distinct (though related) exposure paths: Section 442-c narrows when a broker is vicariously liable purely for a salesperson's specific violation (requiring actual knowledge or retained benefit after notice), while Section 175.21 independently requires the broker to actively supervise in the first place -- a broker who never meets 442-c's knowledge/benefit threshold can still face discipline under 175.21 for failing to supervise adequately.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-c; 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (interaction of the two standards)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A salesperson's association with Broker A ends on a Monday, and the salesperson begins working with Broker B the following week without any gap being reported. Under RPL Section 442-b, which broker(s) have a reporting obligation to DOS?
choice_a: Both -- Broker A must report the discontinuance, and Broker B must separately report the new association
choice_b: Only Broker B, since Broker A's relationship with the salesperson has already ended
choice_c: Only the salesperson has any reporting duty; neither broker is required to report anything
choice_d: Neither broker has any reporting duty as long as the gap is less than one month
explanation: RPL Section 442-b creates reporting duties on both sides of a salesperson's transition: the broker being left must report the discontinuance, and the new broker must separately report the change of association (accompanied by the one-dollar fee) -- ensuring DOS's licensing records accurately reflect current supervisory relationships at all times.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-b (applied -- dual reporting duty)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A broker, aware that a particular salesperson has a documented pattern of overstepping the unauthorized-practice-of-law limits, takes no additional training or corrective steps and later discovers the salesperson has done it again on a new deal. Which of the following most directly reflects the broker's compliance exposure?
choice_a: The broker's own knowledge of the pattern and failure to correct it strengthens both an actual-knowledge argument under Section 442-c and a failure-to-supervise argument under Section 175.21
choice_b: The broker has no exposure whatsoever, since only the individual salesperson who overstepped can ever face discipline
choice_c: The broker's exposure depends solely on whether the salesperson has more than five years of experience
choice_d: The broker's exposure is eliminated entirely as long as the brokerage carries general liability insurance
explanation: A documented pattern the broker was aware of but did nothing about strengthens both the 'actual knowledge' basis for discipline under Section 442-c and a separate failure-to-supervise theory under Section 175.21's regular-frequent-consistent oversight standard -- the two theories can reinforce each other on the same facts.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-c; 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (applied, composite scenario)
